title: What Helps Denoising Can Hurt Memory: Rethinking History in Long Video Generation

paper.title: What Helps Denoising Can Hurt Memory: Rethinking History in Long Video Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract Autoregressive video generators produce long videos block by block, using historical context to maintain temporal consistency. After denoising, a committing pass encodes each clean block into keys and values (KV) that later blocks read, and the same clean block can be encoded into different KV depending on the history it reads. We therefore study historical context not only as a condition for denoising but also as an input to committing. Older historical context that supports denoising can harm subsequent generation when read during committing. At fixed context size and temporal positions, older historical context lowers mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency. Across 5 generator configurations supporting longer contexts, consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines as committing context expands. Motivated by these findings, we propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. During committing, each block reads only the preceding block’s stored KV, so older historical context reaches new entries only through the chain. We apply this rule to 6 pretrained generators. On 60-second VBench, Commit Forcing improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 Quality points and 1.10 Total points. Long-range consistency gains extend to 240-second videos. In a blinded comparison on 120-second LongLive videos, Commit Forcing achieves win rates of 83.5% for subject and scene consistency and 82.9% for overall preference against the base generator, excluding ties.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Video diffusion models can generate realistic videos with coherent motion [ 21 ] . Conventional bidirectional models jointly denoise short windows, with dense attention costs growing quadratically with window length [ 28 ] . CausVid distills a pretrained bidirectional model into an autoregressive generator that produces successive blocks conditioned on historical context [ 28 ] . During inference, autoregressive generators reuse historical context through persistent key-value (KV) caches, reducing repeated computation over past frames [ 7 ] . Within a limited cache budget, Self-Forcing (SF) keeps recent historical context in a rolling window. LongLive uses initial-frame context as a persistent sink to condition later blocks [ 8 , 27 ] . At inference, each block is generated through a few denoising steps conditioned on cached historical context. A separate forward pass on the resulting clean block then writes its keys and values into the KV cache, the memory that later blocks read [ 8 ] . We refer to these stages as denoising and committing. Prior work also calls this pass cache writing [ 7 ] or KV cache update. Each block therefore uses historical context in two stages, during denoising to generate the block and during committing to write the memory. Because committing attends to this history, the KV cache entry written for the same clean block depends on which history committing reads. Existing methods differ in which history they read during committing and how they train or update KV caches [ 15 , 18 , 26 , 31 ] . However, these works do not systematically study which historical context committing should read, or how much of it. In this work, we study historical context not only as a condition for denoising but also as an input to committing. History useful for denoising is not necessarily useful for committing, whose output conditions later blocks. As the controlled interventions in Table 1 show, older historical context that benefits denoising can impair subsequent generation when read during committing. At fixed context size and temporal positions, reading older historical context during committing lowers mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency on Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) [ 31 ] and LongLive. Across committing-window scans on 5 generator configurations, we detect a rise, a plateau, and then a decline in consistency as the window widens. The rise comes with reduced motion, consistent with temporal smoothing during committing, and the decline is consistent with direct reads of older historical context. Motivated by these findings, we propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Each committing pass reads only the preceding block’s stored KV, so older historical context reaches new entries only through the chain. We keep the base historical context for denoising, including the sink, where it is beneficial. We apply this rule to 6 pretrained generators without retraining or additional DiT forward passes. On 60-second VBench, Commit Forcing improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 and 1.10 points. Clip-to-clip Subject Consistency gains extend to 240-second videos, reaching 5.42 points on SGF. In a blinded 120-second comparison on LongLive, Commit Forcing achieves win rates of 83.5% for subject and scene consistency and 82.9% for overall preference, excluding ties. Our contributions are as follows: • We show that historical context can have opposing effects in the two stages of autoregressive video generation. Older historical context that helps denoising can harm subsequent generation when read during committing, even in generators trained to read it there. • We characterize which historical context committing should read, and how much of it. Older historical context lowers consistency even at fixed context size and positions. Across 5 generator configurations supporting longer contexts, consistency rises, plateaus, and declines as the committing window widens. • We propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. It improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators by up to 1.27 Quality points and 1.10 Total points, extends consistency gains to 240-second videos, and achieves an 82.9% win rate in overall human preference on LongLive.

sections.heading: Autoregressive video training.
sections.text: Teacher forcing trains autoregressive models on clean reference context [ 8 ] . Diffusion Forcing adds per-frame noise to this context to bring training closer to autoregressive inference [ 2 ] . However, reference context, even when noised, differs from the model’s own past outputs during autoregressive rollout, creating exposure bias. Self-Forcing reduces exposure bias by training on self-generated rollouts but still distills from a bidirectional teacher [ 8 ] . Causal Forcing uses an autoregressive teacher for ODE initialization, addressing the architectural mismatch between teacher and student [ 30 ] .

sections.heading: Retaining historical context.
sections.text: Caching historical context as clean KV avoids recomputing past-frame representations at each denoising step [ 7 ] . In long self-generated videos, the student’s rollout can exceed the teacher’s temporal horizon, creating a supervision mismatch [ 4 , 3 ] . Context Forcing (CF) extends the teacher’s context to supervise a long-context student [ 3 ] , whereas Self-Forcing++ supervises short segments sampled from long rollouts [ 4 ] . To limit cache size as videos grow longer, LongLive, Rolling Sink, and CF combine recent windows with persistent or refreshed sinks [ 27 , 13 , 3 ] . Other methods keep or retrieve selected older historical context beyond the recent window [ 5 , 25 , 29 , 17 ] , or improve memory efficiency [ 22 , 16 , 11 , 14 ] .

sections.heading: Historical context during denoising and committing.
sections.text: In CausVid and Self-Forcing, committing reads the same historical context as denoising [ 28 , 8 ] . Some later methods change what each stage reads. Rolling Forcing reads the sink during denoising but not during committing in training [ 15 ] , and ID-Forcing uses self-only committing, which reads no historical KV, to match training configurations [ 18 ] . Recency Forcing (RF) reweights historical attention during denoising [ 1 ] , and TetherMem routes it by memory age without retraining [ 12 ] . Others train committing directly. SGF backpropagates losses from later blocks through committing [ 31 ] , SGF+ separates the parameters of the two stages [ 19 ] , and Uncertainty DMD perturbs clean blocks before committing [ 6 ] . Cache designs further reduce committing passes [ 24 ] or adapt cached KV to the denoising timestep [ 26 , 23 ] . Unlike these methods, we keep the weights fixed and use controlled interventions to characterize which historical context committing should read, including on LongLive, whose training includes the sink in committing. We then apply the resulting rule, Commit Forcing, to 6 generators.

sections.heading: 3 Mechanistic Analysis
sections.text: To characterize which historical context committing should read, we change what each stage reads in pretrained generators and keep all weights fixed. We compare the effects of the sink in denoising and committing, and vary the source, position, recency, and amount of the context read during committing.

sections.heading: 3.2 Source Effects
sections.text: To test whether the sink harms committing through its content or its initial temporal position, we vary the source and positions of three historical frames in LongLive’s committing context, with the context size and denoising fixed. As shown in Table 2 , sink KV raises Drift from 0.033 to 0.051 at the initial positions and to 0.102 at recent positions, whereas moving recent KV to the initial positions has no significant effect. The initial position therefore does not account for the sink’s harm, which persists at both positions with a size that depends on position. The same holds on other generators at an unchanged context size. Replacing sink KV with recent KV in a 9-frame context on SGF improves Quality by 1.25 points and clip-to-clip Subject Consistency by 4.54 points, as shown in Table A.10 , and replacing replayed KV with recent KV on Rolling Sink raises Consistency from 0.1434 to 0.1540 and the late-to-early motion ratio by 18.3%, as reported in Appendix A.2 . sections.heading: 3.3 Recency Trade-off
sections.text: Figure 2 : Mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency (Subject c2c , 0–100 scale) against the lag d d of the historical KV read during committing. We fill the three historical frames in the committing context with KV from d d blocks earlier in the original trajectory to test whether older historical context does more harm during committing. We vary d ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 } d\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} , always include the three current frames, and keep all assigned temporal positions fixed. As shown in Figure 2 , increasing d d from 1 to 16 significantly reduces mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency by 0.69 points on SGF and 2.46 points on LongLive. Dynamic Degree increases by 5.03 points on SGF and 3.57 points on LongLive, while Quality changes by less than 0.25 points. We repeat this comparison over the same values of d d with the generated video held fixed, so that only the committing context differs across d d . For each d d , we rebuild the SGF cache from the same clean latents and generate only the next block at 5 points in the video. The similarity of the generated block to the opening still decreases significantly, by 0.0010 from d = 1 d=1 to d = 16 d=16 , as shown in Appendix A.5 . The effect on a single block is small. The larger differences in free generation are consistent with feedback through generated latents, as reported in Appendix A.6 .

sections.heading: 3.4 Committing Window
sections.text: To characterize how the amount of recent context read during committing affects consistency, we vary the committing-context size, which we have held fixed so far. On LongLive, committing reads KV from zero to three preceding blocks, with denoising unchanged. As shown in Figure 3 , mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency rises from 86.21 with zero preceding blocks to 87.21 with one, stays at 87.23 with two, and falls to 86.93 with three. Committing with one preceding block exceeds the base by 1.20 points. Figure 3 : Mean LongLive clip-to-clip Subject Consistency (Subject c2c , 0–100 scale) as committing reads KV from more preceding blocks, with denoising unchanged. Orange points mark the plateau at one and two preceding blocks. The dashed line marks the base, which reads sink KV and KV from two preceding blocks. Reading one preceding block raises consistency and lowers Dynamic Degree by 3.63 points. As shown in Figure A.2 , spatially averaging the preceding block’s contribution to the committing attention output reduces both effects together, retaining 29% to 55% of the consistency gain and 37% to 61% of the motion suppression. Extra KV from older blocks during denoising does not reproduce the consistency gain, with clip-to-clip Subject Consistency changes between − 0.23 -0.23 and + 0.09 +0.09 points, none significant, as shown in Appendix A.3 . These results support a temporal-smoothing interpretation of the consistency gain from reading the preceding block. The plateau is consistent with older historical context already reaching new KV through the preceding entry. Fixed-latent interventions on SGF confirm that this dependency exists and decays over the next three blocks, as reported in Appendix A.7 . The decline at three preceding blocks agrees with the finding in Section 3.3 , where older historical context lowers consistency at a fixed context size.

Base (SGF) reads sink S S and two preceding entries. Self-only reads no historical KV, and Commit Forcing reads only the preceding entry. Crosses mark stored historical KV not read during committing. We propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule for long video generation, as illustrated in Figure 4 . It changes only which stored entries committing reads. We keep the base historical context, including the sink, for denoising, where this history is beneficial, as shown in Table 1 . In the notation of Eq. 1 , R b = { b − 1 } , KV b = ℱ θ c ​ ( x b , { KV b − 1 } ) , b ≥ 1 , R_{b}=\{b-1\},\qquad\mathrm{KV}_{b}=\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{c}}_{\theta}\bigl(x_{b};\{\mathrm{KV}_{b-1}\}\bigr),\qquad b\geq 1, (4) and the first block has no historical input. The preceding block enters as its stored KV entry rather than being re-encoded with the current block. The stored entries thus form a chain, in which each new entry reads exactly one existing entry directly. Reading one preceding block retains history-conditioned KV construction while excluding direct reads of older entries. The preferred window depends on the generator and its denoising policy. For the configurations in Table 5 and the pooled SF-with-sink comparison, reading one preceding block is within 0.51 points of the highest tested mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency. All 6 main generators commit blocks of three latent frames, about 0.75 seconds of video, and we define the rule at this block size. Base committing also reads the sink S S in every pass, which gives the sink a direct path to every entry. Commit Forcing removes this direct path but keeps sink KV stored for denoising. sections.heading: Generators.
sections.text: We evaluate SGF, SGF+, CF, LongLive, Rolling Sink, and a training-free RF reproduction (RF-TF), as listed in Table 3 . All 6 are Wan-based and use persistent KV with an explicit committing pass. We apply Commit Forcing to all 6, so committing reads the current block and the preceding block’s stored KV, 6 latent frames in total. Within each base-generator comparison, we use the same denoising and sampler settings and pair outputs by prompt. We also compare with ID-Forcing on SF and LongLive. Appendix B.1 details contexts, noise pairing, and baseline sources.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: On the standard VBench suite [ 9 ] , which covers 16 dimensions, we generate 946 videos of 60 seconds per condition and report official VBench-Long Quality, Semantic, and Total scores [ 10 ] . On the 200 prompts selected in Rolling Forcing [ 15 ] , we evaluate the same generators and SF with a sink at 60 seconds. We also test selected generators at 120 and 240 seconds. The main evaluations use 16 fps and 832 × \times 480 resolution. For the other prompt sets, we compute Quality from its 7 dimensions with VBench’s published normalization and weights, and report it separately. We measure long-range consistency with the clip-to-clip component of VBench-Long Subject Consistency. Appendix B.2 gives scoring, statistical, and protocol details.

sections.text: We compare Commit Forcing with base LongLive and complete ID-Forcing in blinded pairwise evaluations, as shown in Table 4 . sections.heading: 5.3 Long-Horizon Generation
sections.text: To test whether the gains last beyond 60 seconds, we generate 240-second videos on SGF and CF from 32 extended MovieGen prompts. Clip-to-clip Subject Consistency improves by 5.42 points on SGF and 2.23 points on CF, with no significant Quality change on either. For LongLive, we use ID-Forcing’s 128-prompt MovieGen list. Both Quality and clip-to-clip Subject Consistency improve over base LongLive at 120 and 240 seconds. Figure 5 compares base generation with Commit Forcing on SGF and CF. Appendix B.5 reports the full results. Figure 5 : Base generation and Commit Forcing on 240-second videos from the same prompt and initial noise. At 238 seconds, circles mark the church, which changes in the base SGF video, and an extra tool handle that appears only in the base CF video. Appendix B.5 gives selection details.

sections.heading: Comparison with self-only committing.
sections.text: To test whether reading the preceding block is needed, we compare Commit Forcing with self-only committing, which reads no historical KV. Commit Forcing improves clip-to-clip Subject Consistency by 4.93 points on SF with a sink and by 2.51 points on RF-TF, where Quality also rises by 0.24 points. On LongLive, the gain is significant at all three durations, 1.00 to 1.18 points at 60 seconds and 1.30 and 1.31 points at 120 and 240 seconds. On the LongLive standard suite, Commit Forcing also scores significantly higher in 5 of the 7 Quality dimensions, including Subject and Background Consistency. These gains come with lower Dynamic Degree, and LongLive Quality is 0.17 and 0.21 points lower than with self-only committing at 120 and 240 seconds. SGF, SGF+, and CF show no significant consistency gain over self-only committing, as shown in Appendix B.6 .

sections.heading: Committing-window effects.
sections.text: To test whether the window pattern in Section 3.4 holds on other generators, we vary their committing windows with denoising unchanged, as shown in Table 5 . Denser window scans show consistency plateaus at 6–12 and 6–9 frames, respectively. sections.heading: Scope of the rule.
sections.text: SF with a sink favors a wider context, with a consistency plateau at 9–12 frames. SF with a sink and RF-TF share weights, cache, and committing, and differ only in RF’s reweighting of historical attention during denoising. The start of the plateau therefore also depends on the denoising policy. Framewise SGF, which commits one latent frame per block, also shows an intermediate-window plateau. There, reading only the preceding one-frame block lowers consistency by 0.80 points relative to 6 frames, while 3 and 4 frames do not differ significantly from 6, as shown in Table B.30 . As shown in Appendix B.8 , shortening the committing context of the released Rolling Forcing model from its trained 21 frames to 6 frames instead lowers consistency, and constructing recent KV without older historical context worsens transitions in WorldPlay [ 20 ] .

sections.heading: Comparison with complete ID-Forcing.
sections.text: Within the ID-Forcing framework, we replace its committing context with the current block and KV from the two preceding blocks on SF and LongLive. On SF, this adaptation also changes cache handover and omits tail recaching. At 60 seconds on the Rolling Forcing prompt selection, it improves clip-to-clip Subject Consistency by 2.27 to 2.53 points on SF and 2.05 points on LongLive. Quality rises by 0.20 to 0.23 points on SF and does not change significantly on LongLive. Table B.19 gives its standard-suite results. On LongLive, Commit Forcing exceeds complete ID-Forcing in clip-to-clip Subject Consistency by 4.38 to 4.83 points at 60 seconds and by 7.31 and 8.21 points at 120 and 240 seconds. At the two longer durations, its Dynamic Degree is 11.00 and 12.73 points lower, and Quality does not differ significantly, as shown in Appendices B.5 and B.6 .

sections.heading: Inference cost.
sections.text: Within the base frameworks, Commit Forcing adds no DiT forward passes. In paired timing measurements of the 6-frame configurations, wall time decreases by 2–7% across the 6 main generators. Peak GPU memory increases by 5.6 GiB on Rolling Sink and is unchanged on the other 5 generators. Appendix B.9 reports the measurements and ID-Forcing timings.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: History useful for denoising is not necessarily useful for committing, whose output conditions later blocks. Reading the sink reduces Drift during denoising but increases it during committing, and this harm persists whether sink KV is placed at initial or recent positions. At a fixed context size, older historical context read during committing lowers consistency. As committing reads more preceding blocks, consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines. The rise is consistent with temporal smoothing through the preceding block, the plateau with older historical context already reaching new KV through the preceding entry, and the decline with direct reads of older historical context. These findings motivate Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain and leaves the base denoising policy unchanged. It improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators on the 60-second standard VBench suite, and long-range consistency gains extend to 240 seconds. The consistency plateau varies across generators and denoising policies. Future work could investigate training objectives that distinguish the context read during denoising from that read during committing.

sections.heading: Diagnostic readouts.
sections.text: We use 48-second rollouts for the LongLive and SGF stage interventions, the Rolling Sink source intervention in Section 3 , and the SF switching intervention in Appendix A.2 . We report their diagnostic readouts as Consistency, Drift, and Motion. Consistency. We use a contrastive DINOv2 diagnostic on full-frame appearance. Let u i O u_{i}^{\mathrm{O}} and u i L u_{i}^{\mathrm{L}} be normalized mean DINOv2 CLS features from video i i ’s opening (0.5–2 seconds) and late segment (38–47.5 seconds). We normalize each frame embedding before temporal averaging and normalize the resulting segment means. With 𝒥 i \mathcal{J}_{i} containing videos from the same prompt and configuration but other generation seeds, we compute the per-video score in Eq. 2 . We use Consistency for this diagnostic in the stage and source interventions. The 60-second comparisons use VBench-Long metrics, including clip-to-clip Subject Consistency. Motion. We compute mean absolute RGB differences between adjacent decoded frames, multiplied by 255, using uncompressed values in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . We average these differences over 4–8 seconds and 38–47.5 seconds to obtain the early and late motion values m i E m_{i}^{\mathrm{E}} and m i L m_{i}^{\mathrm{L}} . Drift. We compute mean HSV saturation from the decoded MP4, subsampling every other frame and pixel in both spatial dimensions, and aggregate it into 1-second bins. We average bins 4–7 and 38–47 to obtain early and late saturation values s i E s_{i}^{\mathrm{E}} and s i L s_{i}^{\mathrm{L}} . The per-video Drift and Motion scores d i d_{i} and r i r_{i} are defined in Eq. 3 . We average c i c_{i} and d i d_{i} across videos. For Motion, we report the median of r i r_{i} , where 1 indicates unchanged motion relative to the early segment. We also report the proportion of videos with late-to-early motion ratios below 0.85. Motion decline under this diagnostic does not imply literal freezing, and the diagnostic is distinct from VBench Dynamic Degree. Paired mean log-ratio changes and corresponding relative changes appear in Appendix A.2 . Table 1 reports Drift, the mean of d i d_{i} , whereas Figure A.1 uses signed normalized-saturation differences from recent-context committing.

sections.heading: SF switching configuration.
sections.text: We use released SF DMD EMA weights with 20 prompts and generation seeds 0, 1, and 2. Each condition generates 192 latent frames in 64 blocks of 3 frames, corresponding to a nominal 48-second video. All conditions retain the same 160-frame physical cache without a sink. The raw denoising schedule is [ 1000,750,500,250 ] [1000,750,500,250] , warped with a shift of 5 to approximately [ 1000,937.5,833.33,625 ] [1000,937.5,833.33,625] . The context of denoising step 0 contains the newest 12 trajectory frames, and that of steps 1–3 the newest 160, in every DiT layer 0–29. These windows include the current 3-frame block and use the available frames during warm-up. Historical context is read densely with stride 1 and no additional bias or sampling-mass compensation. RoPE uses the original global latent-frame positions. Cache rollover moves the encoded KV without renumbering or re-rotating it. Each committing pass runs the DiT at t = 0 t=0 on the current clean block and reads historical KV to cover either the newest 12 or the newest 160 trajectory frames in total. The 4 schedules in Figure A.1 use recent context throughout, remote context throughout, remote then recent, or recent then remote. For the switching conditions, the first context is used for blocks 0–31 and the second for blocks 32–63. Block 32 completes denoising before its committing context changes. The newly constructed KV first affects generation of block 33. The nominal 24-second switch location is the latent-time boundary 32 × 3 / 4 32\times 3/4 . For the LongLive factorial study, we use 20 prompts and seeds 0 and 1 at 48 seconds. We cross whether denoising and committing read the sink at a fixed attention-context size of 12 latent frames. A stage that reads the sink uses 3 sink, 6 prior recent, and 3 current frames, and a stage that does not uses 9 prior recent and 3 current frames. Warm-up uses the available trajectory frames. Initial frames leave the recent-only read set once they fall outside its window. The current block is noisy during denoising and clean during committing. Sink KV remains stored in both conditions. For Rolling Sink, we use the same prompts and seeds, replacing the base committing context with the current block and KV from recent trajectory frames at a 21-frame committing-context size. We interpret this comparison as a rollout-policy effect because we observe repeat-run variation.

sections.heading: SGF stage intervention.
sections.text: We use the released chunkwise SGF EMA weights on the same 20 prompts and generation seeds 0 and 1, generating 192 latent frames in 64 blocks. All 4 conditions use a 12-frame KV cache, including a 3-frame sink, with a 21-frame training-position range and top_aligned positions. Each denoising and committing context contains either 3 sink, 3 prior recent, and 3 current frames or 6 prior recent and 3 current frames, 9 frames in total. We preserve the positions of selected historical KV and share initial noise and intermediate re-noising across the 4 conditions by resetting RNG states per video. The reference is the condition that reads the sink in both stages of this 9-frame experiment, rather than the 12-frame read set used in the base SGF benchmark comparison. We use the same diagnostic readouts and 4,000 prompt-cluster bootstrap draws as in the LongLive stage study.

sections.heading: Decomposing appearance similarity.
sections.text: Table A.5 decomposes Consistency into similarity to the video’s own opening and to other seeds’ openings, using the same frames and normalized full-frame embeddings. These terms measure full-frame appearance, including scene content and shared visual drift, rather than subject identity alone. sections.text: We separate the cache read during denoising, D D , from the chain cache read by later committing passes, C C . sections.heading: A.5 Historical recency at fixed committing positions
sections.text: We vary historical recency while keeping the committing-context size and assigned temporal positions fixed. We evaluate SGF and LongLive on rollf200 prompts 0–99 at 60 seconds with generation seed 0. After the initial block, each committing context contains the three current latent frames and KV from three historical frames. We select this historical KV at target lags d ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 } d\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} blocks, or from block 0 in the sink condition. We assign all historical keys to the three temporal positions immediately preceding the current block. We retain the model weights and each generator’s base denoising policy, including reading the sink during denoising. For block b ≥ 2 b\geq 2 , we select historical block h b = max ⁡ ( 1 , b − d ) h_{b}=\max(1,b-d) in the nonsink conditions. The context of block 0 contains only its current three frames, and that of block 1 adds the KV entry of block 0 in every condition. The actual source lag increases during startup until the target lag d d is available. In the sink condition, we use h b = 0 h_{b}=0 for all b ≥ 1 b\geq 1 , so its temporal lag grows with the generated trajectory. We treat the sink as a separate source and exclude it from the target-lag regression. Each target-lag condition is a separate free-generation rollout, and historical KV comes from that condition’s own earlier blocks. We match initial and sampler-noise sequences across conditions through per-video seed resets and generate latents separately under each committing context. This differs from the propagation probe in Appendix A.6 , which supplies the same clean latent blocks to both caches. LongLive’s d = 1 d=1 condition reuses the existing 6-frame outputs under this noise protocol. For each historical block, we use the KV from its final t = 0 t=0 committing pass. We read resident entries from the active cache and evicted entries from an auxiliary store that preserves their committed KV. The active KV caches have capacities of 12 frames for SGF and 15 for LongLive. After cleanup, the auxiliary store retains KV for up to 51 additional frames evicted from the active cache, an estimated 15 GB of KV tensors. This store is used only for the recency diagnostic and is absent from inference with Commit Forcing. SGF stores K before RoPE. In the controls of Appendix A.4 , we select historical KV after applying RoPE and retain its original positions. The recency diagnostic instead selects historical KV from the cache or auxiliary store before applying RoPE at the assigned positions immediately before the current block. For prompt 0 and seed 0 with 48 latent frames, the d = 1 d=1 diagnostic path and the 6-frame SGF rule produce identical pixel hashes. sections.heading: Historical recency with a fixed trajectory.
sections.text: The fixed-trajectory probe uses a separate 20-prompt diagnostic list, comprising indices 0–20 except 5 in Self-Forcing’s expanded MovieGen file, with zero-based indexing. We generate a 48-second reference SGF video with a 6-frame committing context ( d = 1 d=1 ) for each prompt and generation seeds 0 and 1, then fix its clean latent trajectory. For each historical condition, we reconstruct a separate cache by committing the same latent blocks in order, using the target-lag selection and assigned positions above. After blocks m ∈ { 20 , 28 , 36 , 44 , 52 } m\in\{20,28,36,44,52\} , we copy the cache and generate block m + 1 m+1 with matched initial noise and intermediate re-noising across conditions. Denoising reads the base 12-frame context, including sink KV. The generated probes do not enter subsequent reconstruction. This design varies committing context throughout cache reconstruction while keeping the latent trajectory fixed. We measure opening similarity as the mean cosine similarity of three generated-frame DINOv2 embeddings to the normalized mean opening embedding from the reference video. We sample the generated block at decoded frames 0, 5, and 11, and the reference opening every 0.25 seconds from 0.5 seconds up to, but excluding, 2 seconds. This is full-frame appearance similarity, distinct from the own-minus-other-seed Consistency diagnostic. Saturation and brightness changes are absolute relative changes from the preceding fixed block to the generated block, with brightness defined as mean HSV value. The luma boundary ratio divides the adjacent-frame luma difference at the generation boundary by the mean difference at the two latent-frame boundaries inside the generated block. Within-latent luma motion averages the remaining adjacent-frame differences on the 0–255 scale. We average over probe positions and generation seeds within each prompt, then use 4,000 paired prompt-bootstrap draws. Slopes are fitted within prompts against log 2 ⁡ d \log_{2}d before averaging. sections.heading: A.6 Propagation and duration of committing effects
sections.text: The SGF interventions use released EMA weights, a 12-frame physical cache storing KV from 3 sink frames, top-aligned positions within the 21-frame training range, a 4-step sampler, and committing at t = 0 t=0 . Each nominal 48-second video contains 64 blocks of three latent frames. The denoising context contains KV from 3 sink and 3 prior recent frames alongside 3 current latent frames throughout, and the committing context contains KV from 6 prior recent frames alongside 3 current latent frames. Sink interventions replace KV from 3 recent frames with sink KV at a fixed 9-frame context size.

The control always uses recent-context committing. In the intervention, we use sink context only during the committing pass for block b ∗ = 20 b^{*}=20 or 40. The self-only committing control uses three current frames for regular committing passes and adds KV from three sink frames at b ∗ b^{*} . sections.text: We fix the generated clean blocks x 0 , … , x b x_{0},\dots,x_{b} , the prompt, and the temporal-position assignments. sections.heading: Fixed-latent measurement on SGF.
sections.text: We use the released SGF EMA weights, a 12-frame physical cache with slots for 3 sink, 6 recent, and 3 current frames, top-aligned positions, and committing at t = 0 t=0 . We use the 20 diagnostic prompts of Appendix A.5 . With generation seed 0, we generate 60-second latent trajectories of 80 blocks using base denoising and Commit Forcing, then fix the clean latents. We rebuild each cache using committing passes alone, without denoising or VAE decoding. The 4 committing policies are Commit Forcing (6 frames), a 9-frame context with KV from two preceding blocks, base committing over all 12 frames including the sink, and self-only committing (3 frames). For each policy, we compare the control reconstruction with three interventions: • Content change. Block b ∗ ∈ { 20 , 40 } b^{*}\in\{20,40\} is committed from the latent of block ( b ∗ + 40 ) mod 80 (b^{*}+40)\bmod 80 in the same video. All other block inputs are unchanged. We test Commit Forcing, base committing, and self-only committing. • Sink change. Block 0, which also supplies the persistent sink, is committed from block 40’s latent under the same 3 policies. • Single sink read. The sink is read in one committing pass at b ∗ ∈ { 20 , 40 } b^{*}\in\{20,40\} , after which the selected policy resumes. The context of this pass contains 3 sink and 3 current frames under Commit Forcing instead of the usual 6 frames, and 3 sink, 3 recent, and 3 current frames under the 9-frame control. These 2 contrasts keep the context size fixed. For self-only committing, the context of the intervened pass grows from 3 current frames to 3 sink and 3 current frames. For the content change and the single sink read, the paired caches are copied immediately before b ∗ b^{*} , and we measure lags 1–32. For the sink change, we measure blocks 1–79. The directly modified entry is excluded from these readouts. For T ∈ { K , V } T\in\{K,V\} , let T m , ℓ A T^{A}_{m,\ell} and T m , ℓ B T^{B}_{m,\ell} be the control and intervention tensors over block m m ’s own slots in layer ℓ \ell . We compute the dimensionless relative difference δ m , ℓ T = ‖ T m , ℓ B − T m , ℓ A ‖ 2 max ⁡ ( ‖ T m , ℓ A ‖ 2 , 10 − 12 ) . \delta^{T}_{m,\ell}=\frac{\|T^{B}_{m,\ell}-T^{A}_{m,\ell}\|_{2}}{\max\!\left(\|T^{A}_{m,\ell}\|_{2},10^{-12}\right)}. Both tensors are converted to float32 before comparison, and the norm covers all selected tokens, heads, and channels. K and V are normalized separately. Layer-mean KV differences average the K and V values across all 30 layers. For the single sink read, we report the layer-mean V difference. For the content change and the single sink read, we average the two intervention positions within each prompt before averaging prompts. Intervals use 4,000 prompt-bootstrap draws, keeping both positions within each sampled prompt. The content and sink changes give 3 × 1,280 3\times 1{,}280 and 3 × 1,580 3\times 1{,}580 entry comparisons, respectively. Each of the 8,580 comparisons covers 30 layers. As shown in Figure A.4 , no excluded layer differs from its control. In every entry, the first changed layer equals the bound. After a content change, Commit Forcing first changes KV for block b ∗ + d b^{*}+d in layer d d , giving no difference from lag 30 onward. Base committing first changes it in layer ⌈ d / 2 ⌉ \lceil d/2\rceil and still differs by 0.0052 at lag 32. Self-only committing leaves all subsequent entries unchanged. After a sink change, the altered sink is read again in every block under base committing, and the mean difference over blocks 1–79 is 0.29. Under Commit Forcing, the difference is 0.42 at block 1, 0.023 at block 5, 0.0088 at block 10, and exactly 0 from block 30. After a single sink read, the next entry’s V differs by 0.28 with Commit Forcing, followed by 0.13, 0.055, and 0.028 over the next three blocks. The difference is exactly 0 from lag 29 onward. The cutoff differs from the content change because changing a committing read leaves the intervened block’s layer-0 KV unchanged. With KV from two preceding blocks, the difference remains 0.007 at lag 32. Self-only committing gives exactly 0 for every subsequent entry in all three interventions. sections.heading: B.1 Generators and baselines
sections.text: We generate benchmark videos at 16 fps and 832 × \times 480 resolution. The main comparison includes 6 generators: SGF, SGF+, CF, LongLive, Rolling Sink, and RF-TF. We use released weights, pair outputs by prompt, and retain each base generator’s cache and sampler configuration. Table B.1 specifies the RF implementations. For all 6 generators in the standard-suite main comparison, the committing context contains the current 3-frame block and the stored KV of the immediately preceding 3-frame block, for 6 latent frames in total. On CF, the historical KV comes from the three committed frames in the fast FIFO. The denoising policy is unchanged. Supporting comparisons use the contexts specified with each result. The comparisons on Rolling Forcing’s 200-prompt selection, denoted rollf200 [ 15 ] , use the same 6-frame context, including SF with a sink. Wider-window references use 9 frames on SGF and SGF+ and 21 on RF-TF, Rolling Sink, and SF with a sink. LongLive uses 6 frames with a separate 12-frame control. CF’s full rule uses 6 frames. The separate ID-Forcing adaptations use 9 frames. The supporting SF comparisons add a sink to the base SF configuration. On CF, we exclude sink KV, slow memory, and stale slots from committing, with separate sink-only and slow-memory-only exclusions as ablations. Stale slots hold non-promoted historical KV outside the fast FIFO while slow memory is still filling. For newly generated videos in the original context-control comparisons, we generate noise in CUDA bfloat16 and preserve each sampler’s RNG behavior. We reset RNG states per prompt and verify paired noise fingerprints. Those comparisons reuse existing SGF, RF-TF, and CF videos from the same input and scoring protocol. We verify their stored prompt identities and generation seeds, but full historical RNG-state and noise fingerprints are unavailable. For the reused SGF outputs, noise is initialized with a CPU torch.Generator seeded by seed * 100003 + idx , where idx is the prompt index. Subsequent torch.randn_like calls use the device’s default RNG. Intermediate-noise matching cannot therefore be verified for these historical outputs. The 6-frame standard-suite arms retain the corresponding reference weights, prompt list, generation seeds, sampler, denoising context, and scoring protocol. Noise pairing follows the protocols above. The SGF comparison retains prompt-level pairing. The standard suite uses Wan2.1-augmented generation prompts for all 946 official VBench entries, corresponding to 944 distinct original prompt strings. Each arm generates one video per entry with generation seed 0 and 957 RGB frames. We preserve the original metadata, including dimension assignments for repeated prompts, and evaluate all 16 dimensions on their designated subsets. The standard-suite SGF+ comparison uses the released chunkwise configuration with a 12-frame cache, 3 sink frames, a 12-frame training-position range, and contiguous temporal positions. We retain SGF+’s separate committing parameters. The supporting rollf200 comparisons use 6- and 9-frame committing contexts, a 21-frame training-position range, and top-aligned positions while retaining a 12-frame cache. We report these configurations separately from the standard suite. In the standard-suite LongLive comparison, we retain the base 12-frame physical cache, including the 3-frame sink KV. The denoising context contains the sink and the newest 9 trajectory frames, whereas the committing context of Commit Forcing contains only the newest 6, comprising 3 prior recent and 3 current frames. The 12-frame committing-window ablation uses a 15-frame KV cache to store the sink alongside KV from 12 trajectory frames. In the custom-input rollf200 and long-video comparisons, both committing policies use a 15-frame physical cache. We use ID-Forcing at revision 4cd6a4c . We evaluate the complete method and the 9-frame recent-context adaptation with the same sink KV storage, conditioning window, and position re-rotation. These adaptations are separate framework comparisons. On SF, we retain the base KV for blocks 5 and 6 at handover and omit ID-Forcing’s per-block tail recaching, changing both committing and cache handover. In both adaptations, the committing context contains the 3-frame current block and KV from 6 recent historical frames. Forward-pass counts for these adaptations and cache capacities for cost measurements appear in Appendix B.9 . Within the base generator frameworks, we preserve the number of DiT forward passes. For the separate 120- and 240-second comparisons on ID-Forcing’s 128-prompt MovieGen list, we use generation seed 0 with our per-prompt noise initialization. We evaluate the 6-frame LongLive committing context at both durations and include the 12-frame context as an ablation. The 240-second LongLive comparisons contain 128 complete videos per arm, with 960 latent frames per video. The authors’ released inference instead fixes the noise seed at 1356145.

sections.heading: B.2 Evaluation protocols and scoring
sections.text: We display benchmark scores on a 0–100 scale and compute all differences and confidence intervals before rounding. Unless stated otherwise, paired comparisons use prompt-bootstrap 95% intervals. An asterisk on a paired difference indicates that its interval excludes 0. We use VBench-Long at commit 45e79ec . We enable --dev_flag and evaluate the standard suite in long_vbench_standard mode with dimension-specific clip lengths and static filtering for Temporal Flickering. We retain the official clip and video aggregation, valid-output denominators, and Subject/Background fusion. We compute Quality, Semantic, and Total with cal_final_score.py , using the official normalization and a 4:1 Quality-to-Semantic weighting. For paired 95% intervals, we use 4,000 joint bootstrap draws over the 944 distinct original prompt strings with bootstrap seed 20261011. Each draw resamples prompt clusters across dimensions and preserves each arm’s official survivor weights. Subject Consistency and Background Consistency use their designated subsets of 72 and 86 prompts. Temporal Flickering filtering and invalid Color outputs can change the surviving counts across arms, which we retain in the coverage records. For custom prompts, we use long_custom_input . We reconstruct Quality from Subject Consistency, Background Consistency, Temporal Flickering, Motion Smoothness, Dynamic Degree, Aesthetic Quality, and Imaging Quality. We use fused per-video video_results for Subject and Background. We combine within-clip consistency and the mapped clip-to-clip term with equal weights. We report the separate unmapped clip-to-clip Subject Consistency score as Subject c2c . We use VBench’s published min-max normalization and weights. We weight Dynamic Degree by 0.5 and each other Quality dimension by 1. For custom-input reconstruction, we divide unnormalized MUSIQ Imaging Quality scores by 100 before using them in the Quality formula. Standard-suite Imaging Quality aggregates are already normalized to 0–1. We omit --static_filter_flag in custom mode and evaluate Temporal Flickering without static filtering. We keep this 7-dimension reconstruction separate from standard-suite Total. For custom prompts, we compute intervals using 4,000 paired prompt-bootstrap draws. All intervals condition on the evaluated weights and generation seeds and do not estimate variation across training runs. Tables B.9 , B.17 , and B.22 use rollf200 with Self-Forcing’s released expanded prompts [ 8 ] . This differs from the first 200 entries used in Appendix B.5 . The 6 Commit Forcing configurations in Table B.9 all read the current latent block and the preceding block’s stored KV, giving a 6-frame committing context. The additional CF component row excludes only the sink. The LongLive controls in Table B.17 use a 12-frame recent context. sections.heading: 60-second comparisons.
sections.text: Each of the three comparisons contains 18 prompt-matched pairs of 60-second videos from rollf200. We sample prompts without replacement before viewing the videos. SGF versus base SGF and LongLive versus base LongLive share one 18-prompt subset. The comparison with complete ID-Forcing uses another. Generation configurations follow Appendix B.1 , with generation seed 0 for videos from the base generator configurations and the prompt index as the rollout seed for complete ID-Forcing. The SGF comparison uses the 9-frame reference. LongLive uses Commit Forcing. For each video, participants view 5-second excerpts from the beginning, middle, and end. Paired excerpts play synchronously side by side, with method identities hidden and left-right positions randomized. Participants judge subject and scene consistency relative to each video’s own opening, allowing normal changes in action, pose, and viewpoint, and give an overall preference based on prompt alignment, visual quality, and motion. Participants can select either video or a tie. The 60-second results aggregate three response sets from 5 participants. Of these sets, two were completed individually and one jointly by the other three participants. Each video pair contributes three responses per criterion, with the joint response counted once. Table B.11 gives the pooled counts, and win rates are wins divided by wins plus losses, excluding ties. The 9-frame SGF reference receives win rates of 75.0% for subject and scene consistency and 74.5% for overall preference.

Five participants not involved in the project answer independently, giving 150 judgments per criterion. Two additional pairs show identical videos. The preregistered rule excludes a participant only if the consistency question receives a nontie response on both identical-video check pairs. All 5 participants are retained. For the 120-second study, 4,000 bootstrap draws resample the 30 prompts while retaining all 5 responses for each sampled prompt. sections.heading: WorldPlay context re-encoding.
sections.text: WorldPlay [ 20 ] uses a HunyuanVideo-1.5 action model with 4 denoising steps at 480p. Before each 4-latent-frame block, it jointly re-encodes the latest 12 latent frames and up to 8 older frames in a noncausal context pass. The older historical context contains the initial 4-frame block and a 4-frame clip retrieved by camera-view overlap. The resulting KV is read during denoising. A persistent committing chain is absent. Our intervention restricts recent-frame queries in the context pass to text and recent-frame keys, while older-frame queries retain all keys. The constructed KV for all context frames is still read during denoising. We use the 10 released test scenes with generation seeds 1 and 2. The three camera trajectories are two full yaw rotations over 40 seconds, a 20-second forward-and-back walk, and a 40-second forward walk. Arms are paired by scene, trajectory, and seed, with 4,000 bootstrap draws over scenes. Final-return similarity is DINOv2 similarity to the opening at the last return pose and uses the rotation and forward-and-back trajectories. Color drift sums the absolute deviations of the late-to-early saturation and brightness ratios from 1, using the last and first 5 seconds. The seam ratio measures frame changes at block boundaries, and the 1-second similarity compares DINOv2 embeddings of frames 1 second apart. A separate 40-frame context-budget test uses the same 10 scenes on the 40-second rotation trajectory with seed 1, comparing restricted and unrestricted context construction at that budget. After denoising, a committing pass encodes each clean block into keys and values (KV) that later blocks read, and the same clean block can be encoded into different KV depending on the history it reads. We therefore study historical context not only as a condition for denoising but also as an input to committing. Older historical context that supports denoising can harm subsequent generation when read during committing. At fixed context size and temporal positions, older historical context lowers mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency. Across 5 generator configurations supporting longer contexts, consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines as committing context expands. Motivated by these findings, we propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. During committing, each block reads only the preceding block’s stored KV, so older historical context reaches new entries only through the chain. We apply this rule to 6 pretrained generators. On 60-second VBench, Commit Forcing improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 Quality points and 1.10 Total points. Long-range consistency gains extend to 240-second videos. In a blinded comparison on 120-second LongLive videos, Commit Forcing achieves win rates of 83.5% for subject and scene consistency and 82.9% for overall preference against the base generator, excluding ties. Gray marks depict dependencies from direct reads of older historical context, and the two later KV entries belong to subsequent blocks. Right: SGF frames at 238 seconds from free generation under each policy, with jacket changes circled. \reportcontents 1 Introduction Video diffusion models can generate realistic videos with coherent motion [ 21 ] . Conventional bidirectional models jointly denoise short windows, with dense attention costs growing quadratically with window length [ 28 ] . CausVid distills a pretrained bidirectional model into an autoregressive generator that produces successive blocks conditioned on historical context [ 28 ] . During inference, autoregressive generators reuse historical context through persistent key-value (KV) caches, reducing repeated computation over past frames [ 7 ] . Within a limited cache budget, Self-Forcing (SF) keeps recent historical context in a rolling window. LongLive uses initial-frame context as a persistent sink to condition later blocks [ 8 , 27 ] . At inference, each block is generated through a few denoising steps conditioned on cached historical context. A separate forward pass on the resulting clean block then writes its keys and values into the KV cache, the memory that later blocks read [ 8 ] . We refer to these stages as denoising and committing. Prior work also calls this pass cache writing [ 7 ] or KV cache update. Each block therefore uses historical context in two stages, during denoising to generate the block and during committing to write the memory. Because committing attends to this history, the KV cache entry written for the same clean block depends on which history committing reads. Existing methods differ in which history they read during committing and how they train or update KV caches [ 15 , 18 , 26 , 31 ] . However, these works do not systematically study which historical context committing should read, or how much of it. In this work, we study historical context not only as a condition for denoising but also as an input to committing. History useful for denoising is not necessarily useful for committing, whose output conditions later blocks. As the controlled interventions in Table 1 show, older historical context that benefits denoising can impair subsequent generation when read during committing. At fixed context size and temporal positions, reading older historical context during committing lowers mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency on Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) [ 31 ] and LongLive. Across committing-window scans on 5 generator configurations, we detect a rise, a plateau, and then a decline in consistency as the window widens. The rise comes with reduced motion, consistent with temporal smoothing during committing, and the decline is consistent with direct reads of older historical context. Motivated by these findings, we propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Each committing pass reads only the preceding block’s stored KV, so older historical context reaches new entries only through the chain. We keep the base historical context for denoising, including the sink, where it is beneficial. We apply this rule to 6 pretrained generators without retraining or additional DiT forward passes. On 60-second VBench, Commit Forcing improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 and 1.10 points. Clip-to-clip Subject Consistency gains extend to 240-second videos, reaching 5.42 points on SGF. In a blinded 120-second comparison on LongLive, Commit Forcing achieves win rates of 83.5% for subject and scene consistency and 82.9% for overall preference, excluding ties. Our contributions are as follows: • We show that historical context can have opposing effects in the two stages of autoregressive video generation. Older historical context that helps denoising can harm subsequent generation when read during committing, even in generators trained to read it there. • We characterize which historical context committing should read, and how much of it. Older historical context lowers consistency even at fixed context size and positions. Across 5 generator configurations supporting longer contexts, consistency rises, plateaus, and declines as the committing window widens. • We propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. It improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators by up to 1.27 Quality points and 1.10 Total points, extends consistency gains to 240-second videos, and achieves an 82.9% win rate in overall human preference on LongLive. 2 Related Work Autoregressive video training. Teacher forcing trains autoregressive models on clean reference context [ 8 ] . Diffusion Forcing adds per-frame noise to this context to bring training closer to autoregressive inference [ 2 ] . However, reference context, even when noised, differs from the model’s own past outputs during autoregressive rollout, creating exposure bias. Self-Forcing reduces exposure bias by training on self-generated rollouts but still distills from a bidirectional teacher [ 8 ] . Causal Forcing uses an autoregressive teacher for ODE initialization, addressing the architectural mismatch between teacher and student [ 30 ] . Retaining historical context. Caching historical context as clean KV avoids recomputing past-frame representations at each denoising step [ 7 ] . In long self-generated videos, the student’s rollout can exceed the teacher’s temporal horizon, creating a supervision mismatch [ 4 , 3 ] . Context Forcing (CF) extends the teacher’s context to supervise a long-context student [ 3 ] , whereas Self-Forcing++ supervises short segments sampled from long rollouts [ 4 ] . To limit cache size as videos grow longer, LongLive, Rolling Sink, and CF combine recent windows with persistent or refreshed sinks [ 27 , 13 , 3 ] . Other methods keep or retrieve selected older historical context beyond the recent window [ 5 , 25 , 29 , 17 ] , or improve memory efficiency [ 22 , 16 , 11 , 14 ] . Historical context during denoising and committing. In CausVid and Self-Forcing, committing reads the same historical context as denoising [ 28 , 8 ] . Some later methods change what each stage reads. Rolling Forcing reads the sink during denoising but not during committing in training [ 15 ] , and ID-Forcing uses self-only committing, which reads no historical KV, to match training configurations [ 18 ] . Recency Forcing (RF) reweights historical attention during denoising [ 1 ] , and TetherMem routes it by memory age without retraining [ 12 ] . Others train committing directly. SGF backpropagates losses from later blocks through committing [ 31 ] , SGF+ separates the parameters of the two stages [ 19 ] , and Uncertainty DMD perturbs clean blocks before committing [ 6 ] . Cache designs further reduce committing passes [ 24 ] or adapt cached KV to the denoising timestep [ 26 , 23 ] . Unlike these methods, we keep the weights fixed and use controlled interventions to characterize which historical context committing should read, including on LongLive, whose training includes the sink in committing. We then apply the resulting rule, Commit Forcing, to 6 generators. 3 Mechanistic Analysis To characterize which historical context committing should read, we change what each stage reads in pretrained generators and keep all weights fixed. We compare the effects of the sink in denoising and committing, and vary the source, position, recency, and amount of the context read during committing. Formulation. Let x b x_{b} be the clean latent block at position b b , z b z_{b} its noise inputs, C b − 1 C_{b-1} the KV cache after block b − 1 b-1 , and θ \theta the model parameters. We treat the cache as the state carried between blocks. Denoising reads it to generate the current block, and committing constructs a clean KV entry for the block at noise level t = 0 t=0 : x b = ℱ θ d ​ ( z b , C b − 1 , D b ) , KV b = ℱ θ c ​ ( x b , { KV j } j ∈ R b ) . x_{b}=\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{d}}_{\theta}(z_{b},C_{b-1};D_{b}),\qquad\mathrm{KV}_{b}=\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{c}}_{\theta}\bigl(x_{b};\{\mathrm{KV}_{j}\}_{j\in R_{b}}\bigr). Consistency thus compares the late segment with the video’s own opening against the openings of other videos. Drift compares mean saturation s s between the early and late segments, and Motion compares their mean absolute RGB differences m m between adjacent frames. We also evaluate 60-second videos on prompts from Rolling Forcing’s 200-prompt list [ 15 ] with VBench-Long [ 10 ] , including clip-to-clip Subject Consistency. As shown in Figure 3 , mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency rises from 86.21 with zero preceding blocks to 87.21 with one, stays at 87.23 with two, and falls to 86.93 with three. Committing with one preceding block exceeds the base by 1.20 points. As shown in Figure A.2 , spatially averaging the preceding block’s contribution to the committing attention output reduces both effects together, retaining 29% to 55% of the consistency gain and 37% to 61% of the motion suppression. Extra KV from older blocks during denoising does not reproduce the consistency gain, with clip-to-clip Subject Consistency changes between − 0.23 -0.23 and + 0.09 +0.09 points, none significant, as shown in Appendix A.3 . These results support a temporal-smoothing interpretation of the consistency gain from reading the preceding block. The plateau is consistent with older historical context already reaching new KV through the preceding entry. Fixed-latent interventions on SGF confirm that this dependency exists and decays over the next three blocks, as reported in Appendix A.7 . The decline at three preceding blocks agrees with the finding in Section 3.3 , where older historical context lowers consistency at a fixed context size. 4 Commit Forcing Figure 4 : Denoising keeps the base historical context. We propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule for long video generation, as illustrated in Figure 4 . It changes only which stored entries committing reads. We keep the base historical context, including the sink, for denoising, where this history is beneficial, as shown in Table 1 . In the notation of Eq. 1 , R b = { b − 1 } , KV b = ℱ θ c ​ ( x b , { KV b − 1 } ) , b ≥ 1 , R_{b}=\{b-1\},\qquad\mathrm{KV}_{b}=\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{c}}_{\theta}\bigl(x_{b};\{\mathrm{KV}_{b-1}\}\bigr),\qquad b\geq 1, (4) and the first block has no historical input. The preceding block enters as its stored KV entry rather than being re-encoded with the current block. The stored entries thus form a chain, in which each new entry reads exactly one existing entry directly. Reading one preceding block retains history-conditioned KV construction while excluding direct reads of older entries. The preferred window depends on the generator and its denoising policy. For the configurations in Table 5 and the pooled SF-with-sink comparison, reading one preceding block is within 0.51 points of the highest tested mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency. All 6 main generators commit blocks of three latent frames, about 0.75 seconds of video, and we define the rule at this block size. We evaluate SGF, SGF+, CF, LongLive, Rolling Sink, and a training-free RF reproduction (RF-TF), as listed in Table 3 . All 6 are Wan-based and use persistent KV with an explicit committing pass. We apply Commit Forcing to all 6, so committing reads the current block and the preceding block’s stored KV, 6 latent frames in total. Within each base-generator comparison, we use the same denoising and sampler settings and pair outputs by prompt. We also compare with ID-Forcing on SF and LongLive. Appendix B.1 details contexts, noise pairing, and baseline sources. Evaluation. On the standard VBench suite [ 9 ] , which covers 16 dimensions, we generate 946 videos of 60 seconds per condition and report official VBench-Long Quality, Semantic, and Total scores [ 10 ] . On the 200 prompts selected in Rolling Forcing [ 15 ] , we evaluate the same generators and SF with a sink at 60 seconds. We also test selected generators at 120 and 240 seconds. The main evaluations use 16 fps and 832 × \times 480 resolution. To test whether reading the preceding block is needed, we compare Commit Forcing with self-only committing, which reads no historical KV. Within the base frameworks, Commit Forcing adds no DiT forward passes. In paired timing measurements of the 6-frame configurations, wall time decreases by 2–7% across the 6 main generators. Appendix B.9 reports the measurements and ID-Forcing timings. 6 Conclusion History useful for denoising is not necessarily useful for committing, whose output conditions later blocks. Reading the sink reduces Drift during denoising but increases it during committing, and this harm persists whether sink KV is placed at initial or recent positions. At a fixed context size, older historical context read during committing lowers consistency. As committing reads more preceding blocks, consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines. The rise is consistent with temporal smoothing through the preceding block, the plateau with older historical context already reaching new KV through the preceding entry, and the decline with direct reads of older historical context. These findings motivate Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain and leaves the base denoising policy unchanged. It improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators on the 60-second standard VBench suite, and long-range consistency gains extend to 240 seconds. The consistency plateau varies across generators and denoising policies. Future work could investigate training objectives that distinguish the context read during denoising from that read during committing.
